title: Saying Thank You
goal: Thank someone for a specific action, respond to thanks, and distinguish gratitude from a literal request or a frustrated reaction.

runs.text: Thanks
is a short expression of gratitude.
Thank you
is another choice. You can add the reason:
Thanks for your help.
Thank someone for helping.
Thank you for waiting.
Thank someone for the action of waiting.
Thanks for the ride.
Thank someone for taking you somewhere.
Thanks for having me over.
Thank a host for inviting you to their home.
I really appreciate it.
Emphasize that their action matters to you.
After
for
, use the thing or action:
for your help
for waiting
. You do not need a long explanation for every small favor.
A practical favor

turns.speaker: Leah

runs.text: Here's the umbrella you can borrow.

turns.en: Here's the umbrella you can borrow.

runs.text: Thanks. I really appreciate it.
No problem.
I'll bring it back tomorrow.

blocks.caption: Name what you appreciate · Leah & Owen

runs.text: Returning a borrowed object is part of this particular scene, not something every thank-you exchange needs.
Thank you so much
and
I can't thank you enough
can express stronger gratitude when that is what you mean.

rows.text: Present the help as something you were happy to do.
Say you enjoyed providing the help or hospitality.
Offer an informal sense of willingness to help again.

runs.text: After dinner at a friend's home

turns.speaker: Owen

runs.text: Thanks for having me over. Dinner was great.

turns.en: Thanks for having me over. Dinner was great.

turns.speaker: Leah

runs.text: You're welcome. It was good to see you.

turns.en: You're welcome. It was good to see you.

turns.speaker: Owen

runs.text: I had a really nice evening.

turns.en: I had a really nice evening.

runs.text: Anytime
can sound welcoming, but it does not have to be an unlimited promise of availability.
No problem
is a recognized response to thanks; do not assume it rejects the gratitude. The same words can reassure someone after an apology in Chapter 9.

turns.speaker: Leah

runs.text: I brought you a small birthday gift.

turns.en: I brought you a small birthday gift.

turns.speaker: Owen

runs.text: Oh, wow. You shouldn't have! Thank you.

turns.en: Oh, wow. You shouldn't have! Thank you.

turns.speaker: Leah

runs.text: I thought you might like it.

turns.en: I thought you might like it.

runs.text: In this gift exchange,
You shouldn't have
expresses surprise and appreciation, not a demand to take the gift away. If you really want to refuse a gift, say that clearly rather than relying on this expression.
After a compliment, you can accept it:
Your presentation was really clear.
Thank you. I appreciate that.
You can give a sincere compliment in return, but you do not have to invent one.
I owe you one
informally acknowledges a favor and suggests returning the favor; it is optional here.

study.title: Optional: The same words, a different intention

runs.text: Thanks a lot
can be sincere. In an explicitly frustrated exchange—
You left without telling me? Thanks a lot
—it can express annoyance instead. The event and delivery change the interpretation. Use a clear
I'm upset that you left without telling me
if you want the complaint to be unmistakable.
Use the complete scene facts below. Practice both people aloud on your own. Start with the models, then cover them.
A friend held the door while you carried a heavy bag. Thank them. They answer
You're welcome
. Finish the brief exchange if needed.
A colleague waited ten minutes for you. Thank them specifically for waiting. They reply
No problem
You are leaving Leah's home after dinner. Thank her for the invitation and say one positive thing about the evening. Support:
Dinner was great
I had a nice evening
Someone praises your drawing:
I love the colors
. Accept the compliment without being required to praise something back.
Your friend helped you move furniture. Give a stronger thank-you. As the friend, acknowledge it with one of the response choices.
Compare two scenes: a friend patiently waited for you; a different friend left without telling you and you were left waiting. Try a sincere
Thanks for waiting
in the first scene and a sarcastic
Thanks a lot
in the second. Explain what each communicates. For the second scene, you can choose the direct complaint instead.
Hide Study. Thank someone for a real or invented favor and rehearse their acknowledgment. Change the favor on the second attempt.
Sample possibilities
Thanks for holding the door. — You're welcome.
Thank you for waiting. — No problem.
Thanks for having me over. Dinner was great. — My pleasure.
Thank you. I appreciate that.
Thank you so much for your help. — Happy to help.
The first expresses gratitude for patience. The second can express frustration in the stated scene, although the words alone do not guarantee sarcasm.
Check:
Did you identify what you appreciate? Did the acknowledgment fit? If your intention was a complaint, would the other person understand that from the context or clearer wording?
